Hemilaminectomy

The two small canine studies report conflicting results for ambulation and postoperative recovery.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

The two small canine studies report conflicting results for ambulation and postoperative recovery.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact category contains two distinct controlled veterinary publications. Draper et al. reported faster return to ambulation, while Bennaim et al. found no significant difference among PBM, rehabilitation with sham PBM, and sham-only groups. These are separate clinical reports, not review articles, and their populations and co-interventions differ. (Draper et al. 2012 Bennaim et al. 2017)

Human and clinical evidence

No human clinical evidence was identified for this surgical indication. The available clinical evidence is veterinary and consists of two small studies in dogs recovering from hemilaminectomy for intervertebral disc disease. The studies do not establish a reproducible benefit across recovery outcomes.

Animal evidence

Draper et al. studied 36 dogs and reported a median time to ambulation of 3.5 days with PBM versus 14 days in controls. Bennaim et al. studied 32 nonambulatory dogs allocated among PBM, rehabilitation with sham PBM, or sham PBM only; no significant differences in recovery-related variables were found. Differences in care and study design limit direct comparison.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No in-vitro or ex-vivo study is listed in the exact hemilaminectomy categories. The available records concern postoperative clinical recovery in dogs.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Draper et al. used an 810 nm near-infrared cluster array with five 200 mW diodes. Bennaim et al. used 660 nm visible red light. The protocols and rehabilitation co-interventions were not identical, and no single dose or schedule can be inferred as optimal from these two studies.

Interpretation

The early positive ambulation result has not been consistently reproduced. Small samples, preliminary designs, and differing rehabilitation protocols make certainty very low. Future trials should separate the effects of PBM from rehabilitation, use a concurrent sham control, and measure ambulation, neurologic function, pain, and adverse events with blinded assessment.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for faster ambulation. One controlled canine study favored PBM, while a second found no recovery advantage.
Publications and records2 unique titles across Surgery > Hemilaminectomy and Spinal column > Hemilaminectomy.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two small controlled canine reports examine postoperative PBM, but their results conflict and their co-interventions differ. One preliminary study reported earlier ambulation, whereas a later three-group trial found no difference in recovery measures. A larger randomized study with standardized rehabilitation and blinded outcomes is needed.
